steps.explanationAfterStep: The arrow runs from the negative chloride to the positive carbon. Chlorine loses its negative charge because it now shares one of its pairs; carbon loses its positive charge because it now has four bonds and a full octet. This is the last step when tert-butanol reacts with concentrated HCl.

title: Chloride and the tert-butyl cation
subtitle: An anion meets a cation: one arrow makes the C–Cl bond
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 5 (Organic reactions)

reactants.caption: chloride + tert-butyl cation
hintTiers: Which species has electrons to give, and which carbon is short of electrons?
The positive carbon has only three bonds and an empty p orbital. One arrow, and no bond breaks.
One arrow: a lone pair of chloride to the positively charged central carbon, making a new C–Cl bond.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Join chloride to the tert-butyl cation.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That methyl carbon already has four bonds; a fifth would give it ten electrons. The electron-poor carbon is the central one, carrying the positive charge.

mechanismSummary: A lone pair of chloride, the source, forms a bond to the positively charged carbon of the tert-butyl cation, which has only six electrons. Both charges disappear: tert-butyl chloride is neutral.
